utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-99-36-T, The Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Appearances -- sorry, Mr. Brdjanin, can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, and good afternoon to you. Appearances, Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. David Cunningham with John Ackerman assisted by Aleksandar Vujic. And I have a couple of logistical matters to bring to the Court's attention. When we broke yesterday, you asked me to estimate how much my redirect examination would be. Probably 10 minutes or 15 at the most. That's the first point. The second point is there was a mix-up solely on the part of the Defence with respect to the proofing of our next witness. We went to the holts that we typically go to. The witness was not there. It was only later that we found out which hotel he was at. We couldn't get a proofing done in the time that was allotted. We're going to go ahead and do it this afternoon and be ready to go first thing with that witness. If there has been any suggestion it was a mistake on VWS's part, that was not the case. It was my responsibility to find out the correct hotel, and I didn't. I take full responsibility for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We expect this witness more or less to be finished with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't anticipate a very long examination-in-chief. It's just going to be how long the cross-examination is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's me, Your Honour, which means it normally takes longer, I agree. But it's difficult to say at the moment because the summary is not very clear as to what he's going to say other than he was wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it depends --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is what I --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- from that. But I would hope that he would finish tomorrow and the whole matter will finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's dealt with, then. THE on-site inspections, visit, have you got anything to report, Mr. Ackerman, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have looked through what Ms. Korner suggested. I had expected she was going to give a list of some places that she thought you should visit. It turns out she is kind of done a travel schedule for you, which maybe a little more than we all needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't seen it obviously. I mean -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps before she became a QC, she was a travel agent. There's a little hint that have here. But in any event, I think the places that she has listed are probably appropriate as at least the full gamut of possibilities. You might not want to go to all of those places. The other thing I worry a little bit about that we need to hash out at some point is just the procedure because what I think should not happen in a view is any of us making representations to the Chamber about what happened in this spot and what happened in that spot. I think at most, you should be told "this is Omarska, this is Keraterm, this is Vrhpolje bridge." But in terms of anyone making submissions at any spot, I don't think it's appropriate. Especially if we don't have a court reporter with us. I don't think we will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I can do is forward the email to your legal officer, Mr. Roberts, so he can see. Much as I'd like to take credit for being as travel agent in my former life, it was actually Ms. Sutherland who produced that. If Your Honours have a look at the proposed places and the actual nuts and bolts of how we deal with it is something that perhaps can be dealt with at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure it will be helpful, Ms. Korner, also because from your side you probably have more experience of -- you are familiar with the area, probably much more than you are. I don't know if you have visited these places already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman I think has been almost as often as we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have been every place, sometimes multiple times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see, I see. So you are in a better position to make an assessment. Then, of course, I will take the advice of those on whom I can rely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as I say, the actual mechanics of how it should work and which places and so on is something that can be assessed later. All we would say is obviously I think the later is can be left within March the better. As Ms. Maglov told you the other day, the weather conditions in Banja Luka, certainly in February, can be awful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I discussed a little bit with Mr. Roberts this morning, in fact, the best timing. And it's probably what we are talking of, we are talking about. So let's deal with it also when we have the short Status Conference that you are proposing to have today after we finish with this witness. It's my wish to -- we are only having this witness now today. We could finish by 5.00, because there is an urgent meeting that I need to attend to. If I can. I mean, I left all options open obviously, but I would like to be present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think there's any difficult with that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. That's perfect. Last thing, let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher can bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Sajic. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you've had enough time to rest and that you are as fresh as a rose this afternoon. We'll try and do our best to conclude your cross-examination, and I understand there's going to be a redirect. So you should be out of here before the end of the day, and then you would be able to go back home. Please remember that you are testifying under oath in terms of the solemn undertaking that you made two days ago when you started giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, as His Honour said, I'll try to finish your questioning today. His Honour has reminded you of the solemn declaration you made to take the truth when you first started testifying here for Mr. Cunningham. I take it that you have been telling the truth the entire time you have been here, you've answered my questions as well as Mr. Cunningham's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to answer that question, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to clear up just something from yesterday so the record is very clear on this. You stated in questioning from Mr. Cunningham - this is transcript 23:6:20 through 21 - that Colonel Vojinovic attended crisis staff meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "The question was did you know Colonel Vojinovic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "And did he attended crisis staff meetings, several of them?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Do you know why he did that the purpose why he was there for?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I think we sat together for one or two meetings. He would usually listen to what was being said. He had no authority to present any of ideas there, to accept or refuse; he just passed on the decisions and conclusions to his command. He was assistant commander of the corps for civilian affairs. So usually he was there on behalf of the civilian affairs organ. But he did not have any powers."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "Do you ever remember any statements that Colonel Vojinovic may have made during crisis staff meetings about what he could or couldn't do?"

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I don't believe he spoke at meetings of the crisis staff. If there was anything he ever said, he would usually just say "I'll just write down what you've just said', but he never made any statements of his own." So just to be clear, Colonel Vojinovic attended ARK crisis staff meetings. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I think yesterday when you were talking about a meeting that he was at, you said there were multiple presidents there from different municipalities. That's a meeting he attended of an expanded crisis staff meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I want to have you look at one document and see if it reminds you of a meeting that you were present for. This is P229. I have a B/C/S copy highlighted. It's not in your book, sir. This is the 7th of June 1992 Sanski Most conclusions adopted at a submeeting of several municipalities. I'd like to direct your attention to paragraph 6. I accidentally highlighted paragraph 5 as well. That's not the one I'm going to ask you about. Read paragraph 6 to yourself, please, and let me know when you've read it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. The part I'm interested in of paragraph 6 is a section which states: "In this respect, we request that the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina provide a corridor for the resettlement of Muslims and Croats to Central Bosnia and Alija's independent state of BH because they voted for it. If the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka fails to solve this issue, our seven municipalities will take all Muslims and Croats under military escort from our municipalities to the centre of Banja Luka." Now, you talked about a meeting where there was an argument with Predrag Radic, and during part of this argument -- I think you said it was people from Prijedor said "we're going to bring all the Muslims and Croats to Banja Luka if you don't do what we want." Is this the same meeting or is this a separate meeting? If it helps you, this is 7th of June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think the question is confusing because this document is not a meeting of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll restate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a document -- sir, it's not an ARK Crisis Staff document. This is a document from -- adopted by seven municipalities together. It is directed to the ARK Crisis Staff, and the threat made in this document is that if these various demands are not met, we will march all of the Muslims and Croats to Banja Luka. Now, do you remember being at an ARK Crisis Staff meeting where that conversation took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I would agree with Mr. Cunningham, because the last part of your question is confusing. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll try again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- instead of saying "do you remember being at the ARK Crisis Staff where that conversation took place" it's "that conversation" which is confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember being at an ARK Crisis Staff meeting where discussion took place on this topic and this threat being made that Muslims and Croats to be brought to Banja Luka? Do you remember a discussion taking place in an ARK Crisis Staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a meeting that I talked to you about when you spoke to me several years ago, and I said the same thing before the Trial Chamber Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. here. I remember a meeting where representatives from Prijedor in a debate, in a polemic - I even remember where they were seated during that meeting - because it was an interesting threat that they had made, I believed. The Prijedor representatives had a polemic, a debate, with the representative of Banja Luka, but I do not remember this being discussed in this specific form. I remember no ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That polemic you've just talked about, the one you talked about yesterday, had to do with the camps in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I remember a polemic between the representatives of Prijedor and those of Banja Luka Municipality. This was about camps or collection centres, and this had to do with Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered the question. Let me now have you read paragraph 4, numbered paragraph 4 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Nicholls. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, on line 25 of page 11, it's reflected "representatives of Prijedor." I believe based on what our case manager tells us that he said "the presidents of Prijedor." And that of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It said "representatives of Prijedor and the president of Banja Luka Municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you say "presidents of Prijedor and Banja Luka Municipality respectively" or "representatives of Prijedor and president of Banja Luka Municipality"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe I've said this before. Representatives of Prijedor and the president of Banja Luka Municipality. The representatives, as I said, were two or three, I believe. They had different duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is that to your satisfaction, Mr. Cunningham? Let's proceed, Mr. Nicholls. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 4, read that to yourself, please. That's another demand of the subregional group which states: "We demand that the 1st Krajina Corps in Banja Luka, and particularly General Momir Talic of the 1st Krajina Corps, purge the 1st Krajina Corps of Muslims and Croats." And it goes on and says that the deadline is for seven days.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is very easy, a very simple question. Reading that, do you remember being at this particular -- at any crisis staff meeting where this demand for the purge of Muslims and Croats from the 1KK was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to give you P1582, please. I have it here. I have virtually all of the documents in B/C/S today. I'm not going to use too many. This is a 9th of June 1KK report on the ARK Krajina Crisis Staff decision. So, sir, it's two days after the document you just looked at. And it states: "One of the issues that was discussed at yesterday's session of the AR Bosnian Krajina Crisis Staff was the general personnel policy in the 1KK." The next paragraph, it states: "An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital and command posts by 15 June 1992." And then it goes on to say: "We consider this demand to be justified." Just take a moment to review that document. I think you'll agree with me that this is another example of the 1KK being briefed on decisions made by the ARK Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, you, as secretary of the secretariat for defence, don't remember taking part in these discussions at all; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, I was still the commander of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. You were also in your position as regional secretary.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very quickly, if I can give you 1583. You can see, sir, that this is a response from General Mladic. It has got the same reference number, 488-3, 9th of June. The response is the same day saying that all officers of Muslim -- officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality must be sent on leave immediately. Now, you know, don't you, that in fact ultimately, not right on this day but soon thereafter, officers of Muslim and Croat nationality were purged from the 1KK; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not trying to deny that, but I do not know the exact date when these officers were purged or who exactly was purged. I don't know the date, whether it was on the same day or not. I can see this order by Mladic, and it looks quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not asking you for the day; I just wanted your confirmation that it in fact occurred, that these men of Muslim and Croat nationality were, in fact, purged from the IKK ranks. Correct? Don't worry about the exact day.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this was something, the purging of the army of officers of non-Serb ethnicity, was something which Mr. Brdjanin had been interested in and advocated for quite some time; isn't that right? Do you understand the question?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you if remember if you attended the 16th assembly session on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Nicholls. I'm finicky about this. You asked two questions; isn't that right? And then you also asked him do you understand the question and he said yes, yes. I don't take it that the first yes is for the first question and the second is for the second. I take it he is asking answering both questions , I take it he is answering one of the questions, so I would like to know which.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I didn't see it, Your Honour. I thought it had been broken up, yes to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, very quickly, this was something, the purging of the army of officers of non-Serb ethnicity, was something which Mr. Brdjanin had been interested in and advocated for quite some time; isn't that right? Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with that completely. Some people from the SDS did have this position, and they were persistent in requesting that. I can't be a hundred per cent certain or confirm this fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about Mr. Brdjanin at the moment. Let me see if this helps you remember. You were at the 16th Assembly on the 12th of May in Banja Luka. Do you remember Mr. Brdjanin's speech where he said, amongst other things, "How can anyone still believe it is all right that we have a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps? I do not think it is."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember -- you remember being at the 16th Assembly on the 12th of May sitting in the front row; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Brdjanin saying the following during his speech at that Assembly meeting: "How can anyone still believe it is all right that we have a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps? I do not think that it is."?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm afraid understand what the question. What is it that you're asking me? Whether I listened to Brdjanin's contribution or -?-

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whether you remember these words being said by Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. As I said before, I did not attend the whole meeting. I was there when General Mladic spoke, but I was not there for the entire meeting. And I have no idea what Vjestica said at the meeting or Brdjanin for that matter. I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Would you grant me that if the transcript and minutes of the meeting are correct and that Mr. Brdjanin, in fact, made that statement, that that would indicate that he was amongst the SDS leadership which thought that Muslims and Croats should be pushed out of the 1KK?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Don't answer yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question because there's a difference between advocating the removal of someone teaching political classes and what he is suggesting, the purging of the entire officer ranks. So to the extent that the question is misleading, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained. Could you rephrase your question because I think there are other ways of putting the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, do you know who this person is being referred to? Who is the Muslim who is teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A teacher at the school, the school centre where officers were being trained, one of the teachers there, the school centre, the training centre. I think the chief of the centre was a Slovene, a Slovene named --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me stop you. You hear Mr. Brdjanin saying that Colonel Hasotic should be replaced; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I think that's a misleading question because even in his recitation of P50, there isn't any reference to a specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We know who it is, so I think it's a fair question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: When you hear Mr. Brdjanin saying that Colonel Hasotic should be removed, that isn't in P50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not argue. Do you remember Colonel Hasotic from the 1KK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was teaching included in his functions, teaching political classes in the army? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did know Colonel Hasotic. He worked in the operations department with Colonel Kelecevic, the chief of staff. And as far as I could tell, they held him in high esteem as an officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was he eventually removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know why he was removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you remember anyone saying that he ought to be removed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the president of the regional SDS said something like that. That's the impression I have, Mr. Vukic. That was the information I had, but I was never physically present when someone actually said that he should or should not be removed. It was just rumour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't go further than this, Mr. Nicholls, and I don't know whether you should pursue the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I can have one more question on this topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me read on a little bit and see if this helps you and helps put Mr. Cunningham at ease. After Mr. Brdjanin said "I do not think it is" speaking about this particular officer, he continued: "I know that people will not like what I'm saying here, but I truly believe in what I say. I am less of a chauvinist than many believe. I merely have a high degree of national awareness, and I believe that in conditions of war, once it is proclaimed, that the entire Serb economy all war planning, all guarding of facilities must be put into the hands of Serbs." And then he continues: "You'll agree that is in line with the types of statements made by members of the SDS who thought that the officer corps should be purged of Muslims and Croats."

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look at P227, please, 29th of May 1992. Sir, this is just, again, much more on this reporting stuff. Now, this is conclusion 23, for counsel, the 29th of May 1992 ARK Crisis Staff meeting. "1, it has been decided that all Muslims and Croats who so wish should be able to move out of the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina but on condition that Serbs living outside the Serbian autonomous districts and regions are allowed to move into the territories of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Autonomous Region of Krajina in this manner in exchange of population..." And it goes on how this will be an organised resettlement of the population under the "family for family" principle. Now, again, if you remember, were you present at the 29th of May ARK Crisis Staff meeting where this conclusion was adopted determining how the population was going to be resettled?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P380. Again, sir, similarly, this is a 1KK report which reports on an ARK Crisis Staff conclusion. This is to the command. It's the 1st of June 1992, and it's the report on the current political and security situation. The third paragraph states: "A portion of the Muslim and Croatian population is moving out, and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures, providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia and places with predominantly Muslim and Croatian populations were also allowed to move out." This is the 1st of June. That's reporting the 29th of May 1992 conclusion, isn't it? You can put them right next to each other if you want. Have you found the section, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found a different document. I think I have a different document here. "Information on the present political and security situation." This is a dispatch that is -- that was submitted, I assume, to the command of the Main Staff because the addressee is the Corps Command. It was signed by the assistant commander for the area, but I don't see any other document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's exactly what you should have. I want you to look at paragraph 3. It starts: "In the Banja Luka region..." On the first page, it's the third full paragraph. Sir, I don't think this should be too complicated. What I want you to do is read the ARK conclusion they're reporting on. You'll agree with me, won't you, that it's referring to the 29th of May conclusion that we just read?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, this information on the present political and security situation, I see it as a report being sent by a subordinate command to a superior command talking about all kinds of things. It starts with enemy forces, and then continues to talk about the situation in the zone of responsibility of its own corps. They're stating that certain things are happening. I don't think this is a reference to any conclusion or a conclusion being carried out. They are stating that some of the Croats and Muslims are moving out, and that the ARK had adopted a decision to make it possible for them and facilitate their moving out. So that's the only potential reference to the crisis staff that I see in this document, but in addition to that, there's nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Exactly. And that's referring to the 29th of May conclusion that we just looked at, isn't it, because they're discussing exactly the same terms? Muslims and Croats are allowed to move out provided that Serbs are allowed to move in. That's what both documents say, and they're two days apart; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a complete dispatch, and this is taken out of context. And I find it very difficult to comment on this simply because this is about communication. This is a dispatch from a subordinate command to its own superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And try to concentrate on the questions because the question was exactly what you said. This is a report being sent up of an ARK Crisis Staff conclusion; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I'm going to object the, and I understand the Court's feeling when I make a speculation objection. But I think it calls for speculation on his part. He's already tried to make the connection and he says he can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He has made the connection. He has answered the question, but there's so much qualifier I just want to clear up the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has answered the question in one respect, but he hasn't actually addressed himself to the part of Mr. Nicholls' question which refers to the ARK Crisis Staff decision. So it's not a question of speculation; it's a question of whether he sees that in the document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is this, to your knowledge and according to you, reporting on the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff, on the relevant decision of the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only speculate as to whether this relates to a decision by the crisis staff or not because it also states "including the region of Bosanska Krajina" and the region of Bosanska Krajina is not the same as the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll move on. I'm not going to let you get off this question yet, though. You tell me the part that you don't understand. The ARK Crisis Staff conclusion says it has been decided that all Muslims and Croats who so wish to be able to move out of the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina on certain conditions. So the ARK has decided that this will be allowed; correct? That's what the ARK Crisis Staff has decided.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The report states: "A portion of the Muslims and Croatian population is moving out and the region of Bosnian Krajina has issued a decision to facilitate such departures." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The ARK Crisis Staff conclusion says that these people will be allowed to move out provided that Serbs living outside the area are allowed to move in; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The report states that the decision to facilitate such departures is taking place providing that the Serbs from Central Bosnia will also be allowed to move; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: These are two days apart; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 1st of June--

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, several days apart.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and the other one is the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, do you still think as wild speculation to think that in this report they're talking about the ARK conclusion? ARK Crisis Staff conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're only looking at a section of the document here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this section is a --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the speakers please try to avoid overlaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we've heard enough on this, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Last question: I think the reason you don't want to attribute to the ARK Crisis Staff and the reason don't want to answer this very easy question is because the report also states those departing would not be allowed to return. That was discussed in the ARK Crisis Staff, and that wasn't printed because that was unprintable, awful thing that nobody would want to have their name on; right? That's why you're refusing to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the form of the question as being argumentative as well as being multifarious, compound question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's a very simple question and I don't think it's argumentative. I think that's why he's not answering the question. And he's under oath, I'd like him to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are again arguing in the presence of the witness, which I don't like. So because of that, let's take this question bit by bit. Mr. Nicholls is suggesting, Mr. Sajic, that you are actually avoiding to answer the question. Do you agree to that, to start with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try to answer part by part. It's not that I'm trying to avoid an answer. But the question itself I'm not sure which capacity you're talking about. This is the corps command, and the other thing is the crisis staff. They have their own systems of reporting. And if I may, Your Honours, may I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whoever wrote this report used their own system of reporting, of writing up reports. They may as well have omitted a number of different things here. They have enemy forces, and the last thing is the situation in Gornji Vakuf, the last item. So they just wrote whatever was necessary to write, and I don't think they included everything that was in the decision of the crisis staff. I don't know why it's not here. I have no idea. I hope this answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't put a question to you. It's Mr. Nicholls who put the question. Perhaps you may go straight to the point, Mr. Nicholls. You referred to one part, and we'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We talked early on and you just restated it that it was important in the military chain of command to have precise reports up and down the chain, and you just explained what goes in is what is necessary; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General Talic sent a representative to ARK Crisis Staff meetings when he did not attend. You've already stated that, and that's true. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General Talic was the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Colonel Vukelic was his subordinate; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a report from Colonel Vukelic up the chain of command; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This report contains, amongst other things, a discussion, a report, on a decision which it calls a decision of the region of Bosnian Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It states that as part of that decision, those departing will not be allowed to return; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, this is, simply put, the implementation -- sorry, let me go back. Just one more question. I don't have the exact page reference, but you'll agree with me that during the time the ARK Crisis Staff met, the ARK Assembly was not meeting; correct? If you need to, we can dig it out of your transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think so. I don't think it was correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So it was the ARK Crisis Staff that was issuing decisions in the Krajina in June of 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what's going on here, this decision, the fact that people are going to be moved out, Bosnians and Croats, and not allowed to return, is nothing more or less than implementation of the Krajina of strategic goal number 1; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the decision stands as you say. Well, whether this is strategic objective number 1 for Krajina, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Let me go back again to the time that you were at the 16th assembly session on the 12th of May sitting in the front row. Were you present when Krajisnik set forth the strategic goals of the Serbian People?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were presented, those goals were presented. I know that there was mention of those goals. I don't know what all the goals were by heart. There were about six or seven, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me refresh your memory. I'm reading from page 13 of P50. This is President Krajisnik speaking. "The Serbian side of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Presidency, the government, the Council for national security which we have set up have formulated strategic priorities, that is to say, the strategic goals for the Serbian People. The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities, the separation of states, separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." That's strategic goal number 1. Do you remember hearing that now?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept that Mr. Krajisnik had said that, but I cannot remember all of it. I can accept that this was a strategic goal. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And strategic goal number 1 is separating the nationalities, and he states that means not being in the same state; right? Well, don't need to -- you've already said that's what he said. Given that that's strategic goal number 1, doesn't it make sense that the decision in the Bosnian Krajina is that those Muslims and Croats who leave are not going to be allowed to return? Because strategic goal number 1 is not to be in the same state with Muslims and Croats; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I make a comment on my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please answer first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's answer first, and then let's hear what your comment is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Which question is he going to answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there's only one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think there's two right there unless I'm reading the transcript wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is doesn't it make sense that the decision in Bosnian Krajina that Muslims and Croats who leave are not going to be allowed to return because strategic goal number 1 is not to be in the same state as Muslims and Croats. This is the question. In other words, you are being asked to confirm that the decision of the ARK Crisis Staff that those who leave will not be allowed to return fits in the first strategic point mentioned or outlined by Krajisnik according to that report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To leave room for those who will be coming from elsewhere, the Serbs coming from other parts. In that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. In the sense that Bosnian Muslims and Croats who leave will not be allowed to return, period, and you're saying the rationale behind that is to allow Serbs to move in; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is linked up in the text. In the statements, it is all linked up. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that makes sense. This whole meeting is about the creation of the Serb State, so it makes sense. I want to talk to you now a little bit about something else you talk about on direct examination, and that is the issue of the camps, the Omarska camp. Now, you stated in your -- well, you talked about how Radic was part of the delegation that went to the camps. And when he came back from the visit to Omarska, he told you about how he felt and it had made him feel bad.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You want me to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm just confirming.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And that is something that you testified about on your direct examination. You certainly talked about that with Mr. Cunningham and the Defence team before you testified, didn't you, the delegation visit to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I guess you told them as much as you could, as much as you knew about that delegation visit, to the best of your memory; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, you know, was in that delegation that visited Omarska; right? And you've --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the statement I made that Brdjanin, Lukic, and Mr. Radic -- Radic did not speak of the composition of the delegation, but I think he was in it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript says Lukic. I think you were said it was "Brdjanin, Vukic, Radic" who were in the delegation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukic, Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. Now, unlike Mr. Radic, Mr. Brdjanin never said to you that he thought that camp was a horrible place, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Radic told me of his impression of the camp. He didn't say -- didn't say much about the organisation of the camp, the state it was in. He spoke of the impression, and this I brought into relation with his past. He said that they were singing Serb songs --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, he said they were singing Serb songs about Greater Serbia, and he found that offensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I please ask you, Mr. Nicholls, to redirect him to the question that you had asked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the question was not to invite you to repeat what Mr. Radic had told you, but whether Mr. Brdjanin -- it's being suggested to you that Mr. Brdjanin never said anything to you that he thought that Omarska was a horrible place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was coming back to it, Your Honour, trying to be a little more precise in my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please. I was just explaining that the question had not been answered, pointing out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Radic also was offended by the prisoners having to give the three-finger salute.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin never told you that the singing at the camp by the prisoners made him feel bad, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He never said anything that he saw in that camp made him feel bad, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. That's what I mean. You never heard him say anything along those lines. And you also never heard him say anything like that, obviously, in any ARK Crisis Staff meeting, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember whether he said something or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you certainly don't remember ever hearing him say anything in the media about how bad Omarska camp was.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show you P284. I've got it highlighted. This is the Kozarski Vjesnik article of 17 July 1992, headline "Krajina representatives in Prijedor." I want to direct your attention, sir, to -- and it states, just for the record: "Representatives of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, Radoslav Brdjanin, president of the war crisis staff" and some others came to Prijedor. And in the part I've highlighted for you, which is on page 2 of the English it, states: "After they had made a tour of the combat areas and collection centres, the visitors from Krajina thanked their hosts for their hospitality." And then it has a quote from Mr. Brdjanin after having toured the collection centre: "What we have seen in Prijedor is an example of a job well done, and it's a pity that many in Banja Luka are not aware of it yet, just as they're not aware of what might happen in Banja Luka in the very near future. Due to the circumstances, there is a constantly growing number of superfluous Muslims in Banja Luka who have fled the surrounding municipalities and are already planning to join the jihad. They are showing loyalty simply because they still constitute a minority."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps while we are at this, the witness might give us his own interpretation or translation of the relevant word in the B/C/S text, in the original text, whether he would translate it as "superfluous" or I don't know. What do you understand by the word which in English is being given to us as "superfluous"? How do you understand that in your own language? How is Mr. Brdjanin, according to that report, describing those Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I haven't quite had time to read through this. I was listening to you, and I had a look. If I may just be allowed a minute or two just read through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Through the relevant section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please do, by all means. Read the whole paragraph starting with "Radoslav Brdjanin said..." Read it to yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, if you have any problem because that text is too small. We can do something about it. I don't know if that's why it's taking you a while. Just let me know if you need us to blow that up or something.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just finished reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry to interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, no, that's no problem at all, Mr. Sajic. Always ask me to take whatever time you need, and we'll grant you that. Mr. Brdjanin according to this report says there's a constantly growing number of what kind of Muslims? How is he describing those Muslims in your own words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it says is a surplus. What that means is that there is a certain percentage of Muslims already in Banja Luka, increasing, which means that Muslims from other municipalities, from the fringe areas, war-torn, fringe areas, and the hostility between the Serbs and the Muslims, and then these Muslims are moving out, which is only logical. People are moving out of war-torn areas. They're trying to escape the war, the war operations. There is a concentration of Muslims building up there, and that's what this word surplus means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That makes it clearer. Now, your question, Mr. -- and sorry for having interrupted you, but this has always been a little bit curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you know as you sit there today that in 1992, Omarska was a terrible place; right? You're not going to argue about that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew a lot more after the war than I had known back in 1992. I was never in Omarska myself, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's why I asked the question the way I did. You know as you sit there today, Omarska in 1992 was a terrible place for the prisoners held there.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And this is the only media report you've seen of Brdjanin's comments. You've never seen this article before, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Brdjanin, having visited Omarska, saying that Prijedor is an example of a job well done, that doesn't surprise you, does it, given his other statements about how only about a thousand Muslims should be allowed to remain in Banja Luka, and they would be old and sweep the streets? It's perfectly consistent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the question is a bit unclear. The camp is one thing, and sweeping the streets is a different thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I can leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we're breaking in four minutes, I'm going to move into one more area. I'd rather just take the break early, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much more time do you have -- do you require, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I hate to say because some questions are taking a long time. About half an hour, I guess, or less, unless things get slowed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can I suggest a limited break of 20 minutes. Would that be acceptable with the interpreters and the rest of the crew? Okay. So we'll have -- and with you, Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Cunningham, and Ms. Korner? Mr. Nicholls, I take it, you accept a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Chuqing, you don't dare say no. So we'll have a 20-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, first, I'm sorry. The strategic goals's quote which I read from P50, that was Radovan Karadzic, not Krajisnik, who made that quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right, sir. I want to ask you just a little bit now about the TO in Banja Luka. You told us yesterday - I don't remember, I'm sorry - what was the years you were TO commander for Banja Luka Municipality? I think it was through the 1980s, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the municipal staff, 1981, and commander since March 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And you went through it - we don't spend a lot of time on it - with Mr. Cunningham. The TO was a parallel structure which along with the JNA in the former Yugoslavia was part of the All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armed forces, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And the idea was really, and you correct me if I'm wrong, that under Tito in Yugoslavia, every square inch of the territory could be defended, in theory at least; that's why you had TO companies. Even down to factories had their own TO companies.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- yes, actually it was every centimetre of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your interview with us - if you want to look at it, you can; otherwise, see if I have this right - the Banja Luka TO comprised about ten companies.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the TO had departments, squads, companies. Some companies had two or three companies, Cajevac, for instance. So the bigger companies had a larger number of units, of squads.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, how many men total could be called up during a TO mobilisation in Banja Luka? I had the impression it was something like 600 to 800 men.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, tell me, then, just, say, in 1991 how many men, if you'd had to call up the entire municipal TO, could you have called up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two district staffs. The municipality was divided up into four parts. Some parts had a smaller population; some had a smaller number of companies, of enterprises. Some were more of a rural nature. The most populated were the enter of the town in terms of number of companies and population, and the number was the largest there. I cannot tell you the exact figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine, just something over 800 men. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More, more. More than 800 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to talk about April 1992 when suddenly there appeared men in Banja Luka who were blocking the entrance to the city. I'm talking about the SOS blockades. You remember that event, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, did you know in advance, before that blockade occurred, that it was going to take place on the 3rd of April?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You looked like you had to think about that for a moment. Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some hints that there was some discontent amongst the soldiers from the battlefields. With the situation in the town, it really existed. But who would report on this, who would make the announcement, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me try to be a little clear in my questions. The SOS in general terms was made up of criminals.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There appeared from time to time people who were criminals, but I cannot confirm that this was a group of criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You do not believe that the men, the SOS men, who blockaded Banja Luka on April 3rd were criminals? To be sure we're talking about the same people.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe all of them were criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. What percentage do you think were criminals?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would have to make a list of those who were criminals and those who weren't. What we judged to be bad was the fact that this was done by people who had a suspicious past.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, you know something about the SOS because you were able to give your assessment that some of them were criminals and some of them weren't. Right? So you know something about who was in the SOS.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- with reference to the comments afterwards. The list of the criminals that you're alluding to, of suspicious people or the list of people who took part in the SOS, I never saw such a list. I don't know who these people were. My impression was that they tended to appear when there were riots or an unstable state of affairs. And they would appear. And this was my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You keep talking about other times. Let's confine ourselves for this conversation to the 3rd of April 1992. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you think that the men who blockaded the town of Banja Luka on the 3rd of April were honourable, good men?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were honourable, good men. I suppose there were some. There was a larger group of people. I cannot single out who was who. I cannot answer that question. There were people who were honourable, and there were others as well. I can't give you a precise answer. I can just say I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Name some of the people, if you can, for me who you knew were in the SOS. I assume you knew some of these people since you know there were some good people in the SOS and you know that there were some bad people.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about someone called Goran, who would remove earrings in a bus where people were travelling. He would remove gold from people. He was prone to crime. But I cannot really invent names. I didn't have the names -- their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you also know, don't you, that a little later on after April, a lot of the members of the SOS became members of the Banja Luka CSB special unit? Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Banja Luka CSB was in a teaching centre, and I don't know the people from there. I have to be more restricted in what I am saying. I can say what I know and what I do not know. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Listen. Try to listen to my questions and answer them if you can. I didn't ask you where the Banja Luka CSB was, and I didn't ask you anybody's name. I asked -- if you don't know, say you don't know, if you don't remember, say you don't remember. If you don't know the answer, say you don't know the answer. Members of the SOS became part of the Banja Luka CSB special unit. Is that right? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said there were hints that this might occur, something along these lines. More precisely, did you have any notice of any plan to blockade Banja Luka in early April?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So when you woke up on the 3rd of April, you had no idea what had gone on and what was going on in the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this when I got up in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got up, when I went to my office, I saw that there was a blockade, and that before the municipality building there were people who refused people to come anywhere near the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How many SOS men did you see personally that day?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, remember, I was in my office that day. I wasn't in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. I didn't ask you where you were. I thought you said that there was a blockade, and there were people who refused people to come anywhere near the building. I thought you were talking about something you had seen.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw about ten people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you see -- you saw those ten people. You saw ten members of the SOS. Let's try to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. You heard during the course of that day that these weren't the only ten members of the SOS, but that other areas of Banja Luka had been blockaded similarly. Right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you got to your office -- you know it's not every day you go to your office and there's a blockade. What did you do when you got to your office? Who did you call to talk about these paramilitary blockades?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the president of the municipality, and I said there was a blockade. And he told me that he had learned about it in the early morning hours, and then he asked for a meeting between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Between whom? Just you and Mr. Radic, or anybody else? Mr. Zupljanin there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. Radic and I were there for sure, and I can't remember about Zupljanin, whether it was Zupljanin or Tutus, I cannot remember. I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The transcript didn't catch it, but I think you said Tutus; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Because I want to...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first floor in the municipality building.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was that in Radic's office?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radic had two offices. There was one, his office, and then an accessory room, and I think it took place in that other room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did Mr. Radic tell you who was behind this SOS blockade? Had he found out at that point?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What did the two of you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we established contact with the police, that this was the first step we took. I think it was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Now, at this point in the morning, at this meeting, you don't know who these SOS members are yet, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Didn't it occur to you as TO commander charged with protecting the city and the Municipality of Banja Luka, that this was something sort of urgent? Armed men -- unknown armed men setting up blockades all around the city?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, my function was not to be commander of the town and not keeping law and order in the town. That was not my job. That was not the duty of the TO units. It was the police, the civilian police who was in charge of such matters. And perhaps my concern was not so great.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. So, say, in 1986, if you'd gotten up one morning, walked into town and discovered that a foreign, occupying power had dropped in troops -- Russia, America, Germany, whoever -- and they were setting up checkpoints, they were armed, you would kind of casually say "this is a police matter, this is outside my jurisdiction. I'm only TO commander with 800 men under me." Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't have mobilised people at the time. TO is a reserve thing. It is not something that existed all the time. It was only the more limited part of the staff that was in operation. It is not an active unit that is in operation the whole day. It was not my duty in that sense, and that is the sense that I understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That sounds reasonable, Mr. Nicholls. Why don't you move straight to what was discussed during that high-level meeting that was convened by Mr. Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's where I was -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At this meeting where you're discussing armed men, you don't know who they are, around the town setting up blockades. It didn't occur to you that maybe the TO ought to be mobilised to deal with this threat, since you had over 800 men at your disposal that you could call up?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it didn't occur to me. Well, the superior commander does this. It cannot mobilise at its will. I don't know what I would achieve by mobilising, because it was the city. Or I don't understand the question. Perhaps you should be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think it was a pretty easy question, which was whether it occurred to you it might be a good idea to have a TO mobilisation when unknown men had set up armed checkpoints all over the city. But I think you've answered that it didn't occur to you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to make sure he understood my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your view was, Well, this is a problem for Zupljanin or Tutus?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the military police, if they were in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, did you call General Talic or your immediate superior or anybody else and say: "Listen, I think you ought to know about this. There were unknown men setting up blockades all over Banja Luka. I've seen them myself. I don't know who they are." Did you make that call?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. It sounds like you weren't particularly alarmed by this; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You mean you were very alarmed. You took this very seriously.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You saw -- you just figured you would wait and see what the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. police did about it? Or the military police?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for the meeting, for something to be resolved at the meeting. I do not have my police forces. I did not have my own forces. I couldn't deal with this with my forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask you this: If Banja Luka had been invaded by a foreign group or army who set up checkpoints, wouldn't that be something within the competence of the Banja Luka TO? That wouldn't be a police matter, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer the question for the simple reason that in Banja Luka, you had the corps command which was the highest command, and the garrison command which was responsible for the entire situation within the garrison. It would have been the same as if, for example, a squad commander had been responsible for the command of the corps because you had two levels of command above me in Banja Luka. And those were the commands responsible for reacting to the situation. My level of responsibility in the sense of using the units was far lower to the level of responsibility of the corps command because they had barracks around Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. So this would have been something that the 1KK as well had competence to deal with; right? You're saying it was the corps command that should have taken care of this.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: General Talic didn't send in a single soldier to confront the SOS, did he? He didn't do anything about it, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you P137. I've got a highlighted copy. This is a Glas article, Saturday the 4th of April, the day after the SOS blockade. It starts saying, and I think I've put the number 1 next to the section, sir, if that helps you. It should be highlighted, but also have a little number 1 next to it. It's the lead story. "Banja Luka, 3 April. Since this morning, the city of Banja Luka that be blocked. Members of the SOS had seized all key intersections in the city and control the Municipal Assembly building, Radio Banja Luka, the Jugo bank building, the Banjalucka Banka, all bridges, and generally all the important strategic positions in the city. "Members of the SOS reservists in the JNA, armed civilians, and as we have heard, men arriving from the Western Slavonia war zone have presented their terms insisting that Predrag Radic form a municipal crisis staff to carry these out." Have you found the part I'm reading from?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In fact, this crisis staff was formed, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it says "in order to set up..."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about what it says there. I'm saying, in fact, a crisis staff was set up in order to deal with the demands of the SOS. Go from your memory. You don't need to read it. Let me help you. There's a highlighted portion. I don't know exactly where it is. It's in a box on there. It says "crisis staff." See if you can find that part. If the usher gives it back to me, I can point you to it. That's quite small print. It says: "Crisis staff. In Banja Luka, after the blockade of the city and presentation of their demands by the Serbian liberation forces - that may be a typo because everything else we're talking about the Serbian Defence forces, SOS - a crisis staff was formed whose president is Predrag Radic." And it also states that Stojan Zupljanin is on that staff. Have you found that section, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were on that crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was founded on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were on that crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the section I was looking at before with you. Now, let's go back to where we were. Going on from how these men are arrived from the Western Slavonian war zone, have presented their terms, insisting the Predrag Radic form a municipal crisis staff to carry these out. And this was done, and after several hours of negotiation between representatives of the SOS on the one side and members of the crisis staff, the Territorial Defence, the JNA's Banja Luka Corps, and from the institutions of the lawful authorities in Banja Luka, all the demands were later accepted, true, in a slightly modified form." That's what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a text from a magazine. May I comment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, you may. But first, I'd like you to answer the question. That's what it says here happened. Crisis staff was formed. There were several hours of negotiations with the SOS. SOS demands were accepted. Is that correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is that correct or incorrect? It's correct? Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, if you want to make a comment, I'm sure His Honour will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just go ahead. And commenting, please, do give us some information on what kind of negotiations took place between the SOS and the Territorial Defence for which you were responsible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The article here states on the one hand members of the crisis staff and the TO, this is a reference to the staff, not the TO. There was no TO crisis staff. The crisis staff had been appointed, which is in the second part; namely, the composition of the crisis staff as given here. That's when it was set up. When they arrived in the office of the president of the municipality, that's when the crisis staff was convened and set up. They insisted on it. I'll give you an example. The president of the executive council of Banja Luka Municipality, he, for example, was not allowed in, and that's he was not a member of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's pretty much confusing, in my view. Were you present, yourself, as head of the TO during any of the negotiations which, according to this report, took place between representatives of the SOS and others, including the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were. Who else was present during those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, precisely the people indicated here. On behalf of the police, these people here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
