utterances.text: All right. And why would the Territorial Defence be part of these negotiations if the head of the Territorial Defence did not consider his role or the role of the Territorial Defence relevant to the situation that arose at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because the president of the municipality had called the commander of the TO in, and the assistant as well as the chief of the public security centre. And some other people, the chief of the police station or whatever it was called, Tutus, and some other people from the municipality who he believed he needed to call. I was not the one who convened the meeting, and I was not the one who decided who the people present would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So basically, although you personally believed that the Territorial Defence had -- did not fit in this whole scenario, whoever called the meeting did not feel that way. He thought that the Territorial Defence ought to be part of the negotiations or to take part in the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really can't know what the person believed. But this is not a scenario. I sat there together with President Radic in the same office, on the same side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let's just run through quickly who was on this crisis staff. Not necessarily all of them, but some of the people. And you can look at the magazine if it helps you remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we see it. Can we have it back on the ELMO, please, usher. Sorry to trouble you like this. It's on the third page, I think, or something like that. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. Page 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have it on the ELMO, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have Predrag Radic. You've already stated that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Dr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, he was on this crisis staff which was formed that day. That's what you're saying? I just want to be clear of your answer.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So was Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yourself.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name, I didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were on it as well. You've already stated that.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nenad Stevandic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Jovo Rosic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Milan Puvacic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All the men I've just read out to you were also about a month later on the ARK Crisis Staff; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the city's blockaded by unknown armed men surprisingly. And quickly in the morning, this crisis staff is set up with these people, representatives of the TO, civilian leadership, and police leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Negotiations are held with the SOS representatives.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who represented the SOS in these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there was a bearded man, Milankovic, Milinkovic. Not sure about the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could we go in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go ahead, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that binder that is in front of you right now is a copy of your statement to the Prosecution in your native language. And I have tabbed -- there are three pages that I have tabbed in there. And I want you to look at a tab that says "55." When you go to tab 55, it won't take you to page 55 in your language, but it will take us to page 55 in the English. And I'm going to -- and there should be a bracketed portion there. Yesterday, when you were questioned by Mr. Nicholls, he asked you about a portion of this page where he asks you whether it was true that Mr. Brdjanin presided over meetings of the ARK Crisis Staff. And as you did in your statement, you answered him with a "yes" answer here. Now, if we were look down to the passage right after that, which is in that -- it should be bracketed on that page that you have in front of you -- you were asked this question, reading from the transcript at page 55: "And isn't it true -- isn't it also true that the crisis staff meetings could not start unless Radoslav Brdjanin was present in the 0011 room?" I want you to read your answer to yourself and then explain what you meant by that. Because in the transcript you said: "I am sorry that I'm laughing." What were you laughing at? Do you have any recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember why I was laughing. But my answer was affirmative.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next topic. The next topic deals with Prosecution Exhibit 167, which is -- I think there's a corrected version of at P182. But this is your order of 4 May 1992 having to deal with, one, mobilisation, and two, disarmament. In the course of your -- in the course of your testimony -- it should be marked 167 if he needs to look at it. In the course of your testimony yesterday, you were talking about a specific example about disarmament. That involved a Muslim colleague of yours that was -- had a rifle that was provided to him and that weapon was confiscated. My question to you, first of all, is do you remember that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember who took the weapon away from your Muslim or Bosniak colleague?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the police officers, the reserve police officers. Someone from the police. I'm not sure if active-duty or a reserve police officer, but it was a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And do you remember whether --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what he told me, according to what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: "He" being your Muslim colleague; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, when your Muslim colleague told you about the officer who took his gun away from him, did he also give you any other information about this officer, specifically whether or not they had any prior meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He complained. I'll try to make this as short as possible. He complained about this happening to him and apologised to me because he had mentioned my name. And he told me that it was one of the police officers whom he had punished some time ago because this colleague of mine once worked with the SUP. He was the assistant chief or something like that. And that was apparently the reason in his understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm done with that exhibit. I want to talk to you about Predrag Radic, his statements to you which indicated that he was upset and distressed by what he saw in Omarska. You've told us that you did not speak to Mr. Brdjanin about this. But let me ask you this: Based on what you know about Mr. Brdjanin, do you know whether he would agree or disagree with the sentiments that Mr. Radic expressed?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose he would have agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Another area that I want to talk to you about that was discussed yesterday at page 86 of the LiveNote. You were asked certain questions about the relationship between the Kljuc Municipal Crisis Staff and the ARK Crisis Staff. My question to you, first of all, is do you remember talking about the Kljuc Crisis Staff yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Who do you think would be in a better position to determine the relationship between the Kljuc Municipal Crisis Staff and the ARK Crisis Staff? You or a member of the Kljuc Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the Kljuc Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I have one question I forgot, and I'd like to go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go back to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sajic, we have some questions for you from the Bench. Judge Janu from the Czech Republic is going first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Sajic, can you tell me how long do you know Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1991 or 1992. Not long. I didn't know him before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: In your statement, and I will read it to you, you said: "As far as my personal opinion of Mr. Brdjanin, I believe that he was a very hard-working and educated man, but he enjoyed power and wanted to assert himself. He enjoyed appearing in the media and in newspaper and on television and the radio, in order to leave the impression that he had more authority than was really the case." When you were cross-examined, you were shown the Exhibit P284. You don't need it. It was Kozarski Vjesnik, article from 17 of July 1992. And in this article, and you spent quite a time reading it, Mr. Brdjanin said something like this. "What we have seen in Prijedor is an example of a good -- of a job well done." And he carry on something like that, in Banja Luka, you are not aware of it yet, and like this. Can you tell me, if you know Mr. Brdjanin well, what he meant by this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what he meant when he said that. But I simply read the article, and I gave my statements. I said in the statement what I thought about him. I know that he was often running about and that his words actually spoke louder than his actions. I can't tell you what he thought, what he meant by saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: What could you see, what could have been seen in Prijedor on 17 July 1992, what Mr. Brdjanin marked as a "well-done job, which can serve as an example for Banja Luka"? You were present at that time. You were living in the same area, so...

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all truthfulness, I was never in any of those camps or centres, and the only impression I obtained on that was from my conversations with Radic. If the conditions in the camp were described as normal, then they were normal; if they were bad, then they were bad. I can't give you a specific answer. Or maybe if you'd care to clarify the question. I don't know what he meant by comparing those two elements. If he meant that the same thing should happen in Banja Luka, then that was insane, because there was no way that kind of thing could happen in Banja Luka, or at least that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: I cannot clarify it more. I would just cite from the article, and I wanted your reaction. So if you cannot react, it's all right with me. And there was a second part, the same -- the same article as -- which said something like this: "There is a growing number of surplus Muslims in Banja Luka who have fled from the surrounding municipalities, and they are already planning to join the jihad." You were at that time commander of TO. Can you tell me, was there any base for such a pronouncement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a statement dated the 17th of July, if that's the statement you're talking about. I was not in that position at the time. As for a jihad in Banja Luka, my feeling was that this could simply not happen in Banja Luka. If he believed there were too many Muslims around, well that's his own personal thing. That's certainly not a position that I share. I hope I've made myself clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Your perception wasn't the same as Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD SAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt. There was a portion that was not translated, with respect to page 74, line 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What the witness said was "that his tongue was faster than his brain," and what got translated was "that his words actually spoke louder than his actions." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sajic, you just heard Mr. Cunningham. When you were answering previous questions a minute ago, did you say that his tongue was faster than his brain, or that his words spoke louder than his actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tongue longer than brains.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. JUDGE Taya, you don't have any questions? Judge Taya doesn't have any questions, and I don't have any questions either, which basically means that your testimony comes to an end here. Before the usher escorts you out of the courtroom, it is my duty as Presiding Judge in this trial, on my own behalf, on behalf of Judge Janu and Taya, Judges Janu and Taya, and on behalf of the Tribunal in general, to thank you for having come to give testimony in this trial. You will, as I told you, be accompanied by the usher out of this courtroom, and you will be attended to so that you can return to your country of residence as soon as possible. Once more, thank you, and we wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, are you still fresh enough to start and finish a quick Status Conference? I don't want to impose on anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I would be grateful if we could postpone it, but it depends really how much is involved. Your Honour has given us the dates. You've had Mr. Ackerman's list of witnesses, which is considerably shortened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The only thing that we note about it is there's a gap at the moment of two weeks, between the 26th of January and the 9th of February. But I understand that's because Mr. Shoup won't be able to get his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That, I understand, is one of the problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the other thing -- the only thing I was going to ask is that we would like to have his report at the latest by Monday, the 26th of January. That's only giving us two weeks, and in fact that's less than the Rules say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's less than the 30 days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll live with two weeks, provided that's a guarantee.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the email with me from Professor Shoup, but in my head I think January 15th is the date that he's supposed to have the report to me. So I think the 26th is easy to do. And I'll, of course, give it to them as soon as I get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think January 15th was the date it was supposed to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as far as any other matters we need to take up on the Status Conference, I think just kind of piecemeal over the last two or three days we have basically dealt with all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's really not much left to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say on this witness list that I've given everybody today that numbers 14, 45, and 11 I would characterise as soft.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only other matter, apart from whether or not the document becomes an exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- can be dealt with tomorrow as well -- is could we have a decision from Your Honours on the question of joint criminal enterprise, the third category, as to whether in light of the appeal all parties should treat it as though it's still a live issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We consider -- shall we come back to you tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I mean. Yes. Sorry, Your Honour, I'm just asking that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to you tomorrow morning. Mr. Roberts, tomorrow morning we'll try and meet a little bit before we start the sitting, say, 15 minutes before, and then conclude all the remaining matters. Do you have the last three pages?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm printing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a very silent printer. Let's go into private session for the time being, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. If you give me those documents, I will have them signed, Madam Registrar. And we can call it a day. Now, we start -- this starts page 78, and I'm missing page 79 completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So for the record, we are redacting from page 78 line 6, right through and including page 80 line 23. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it would be real helpful if you would read the last line that's being redacted because of the way the page numbers are not lining up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me see the last line. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we have concluded our business for today. I thank you all, including the interpreters and the technicians. I had a list of everyone that is helping us, and it's impressive how many people are behind the glasses, the glass panes that we have. I thank you all. Have a nice evening, and we'll meet again tomorrow morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of December, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
